findings.text: fixup_irqs is a public routine used when a CPU goes offline. It first migrates interrupts away, waits briefly, then scans that CPU vector table and either reissues still-pending entries toward their new targets or releases the slots.
The offline vector scan does not take the vector lock. The stated reason is that the CPU is already marked not online, so no other party is expected to touch its per-CPU vector array during the walk.

For a vector found pending, the owning interrupt descriptor lock is held while obtaining the descriptor data and chip, conditionally invoking the chip retrigger operation, and marking the per-CPU slot as retriggered.

Each scanned vector slot starts either empty or associated with a descriptor. Empty or error-marked slots are skipped. A pending slot with retrigger support moves to a retriggered marker, while all other non-retriggered slots end as unused.
The thermal system-vector handler is an interrupt entry that traces entry, accounts a thermal interrupt, runs a small dispatch helper, traces exit, and then acknowledges the local APIC.

Thermal dispatch checks whether x86 thermal handling is enabled. If enabled it runs the Intel thermal handler, otherwise it logs an unexpected thermal local-vector interrupt identifying the current CPU.

The 32-bit CPU stack initializer, the 64-bit CPU stack initializer, the softirq own-stack runner, the IRQ-work raiser, the ISA and general IRQ initializers, and the panic-on-stackoverflow control are visible outside their files for boot and interrupt setup.

32-bit per-CPU stack setup is idempotent when a hard stack pointer already exists. Otherwise it allocates hard and soft stacks on the target node, reports memory exhaustion if either allocation fails, frees the first stack when only the second fails, and publishes both pointers on success.

The 32-bit softirq runner executes softirq handling on a dedicated per-CPU stack. It loads the softirq stack base, reserves the stack object, saves the current stack pointer in the base slot, and transfers control to the common softirq handler on the new stack.

The two 64-bit stack mapping variants both publish a top-of-stack pointer offset slightly below the allocation end to avoid hot-path adjustment. One variant builds a page list from the backing store and maps it, failing with memory exhaustion if mapping fails; the other uses the backing store directly. The 64-bit initializer is idempotent and otherwise delegates to the mapping helper.
The IRQ-work system-vector entry acknowledges the APIC first, then traces entry, accounts IRQ-work, runs the queued work, and traces exit.

Raising in-band IRQ work does nothing when the platform reports no IRQ-work interrupt. Otherwise it sends the IRQ-work vector to the local CPU and waits for the controller command interface to become idle.
vector_irq is a per-CPU table with one entry per vector. Every slot is statically initialized to the unused marker before boot assignment.

ISA IRQ setup initializes the boot APIC path and legacy controller, then assigns the legacy chip, level-triggered handler, and level status to each legacy IRQ. General IRQ setup preassigns ISA vectors on CPU zero, ensures the current CPU stacks exist, and invokes the platform interrupt initializer. Native IRQ setup runs pre-vector quirks, completes exception setup paths, installs APIC and IRQ gates unless in FRED mode, assigns system vectors, and conditionally registers the cascade handler.

The cascade registration only occurs when neither ACPI nor device-tree I/O APIC information is present and at least one legacy IRQ exists. It requests the second-controller cascade line with no-thread behavior and reports failure without aborting boot.
General IRQ initialization treats failure to prepare the boot CPU interrupt stacks as fatal and stops boot.

ITMT support and enable changes are serialized by a dedicated update mutex. Enable writes and support set or clear operations hold that mutex across checking and updating capability state, debug entries, flags, and scheduler domain refresh decisions.

Writing the ITMT enable control only marks topology as changed and rebuilds scheduler domains when the stored value actually changes. Reading core priorities emits a header followed by one priority line per possible CPU.
ITMT exposes an asymmetric priority getter for scheduler use, a per-CPU priority setter, support enable and disable routines, and a globally visible enable flag plus per-CPU priority storage.

ITMT support is idempotent in both directions. Setting support when already capable does nothing; otherwise it creates two debug entries with tolerated creation failure, marks capable, enables scheduling use, and refreshes topology and domains. Clearing support when not capable does nothing; otherwise it clears capability, removes debug entries, and if enable was set, disables it and refreshes topology and domains.

The ITMT debug file table provides boolean read, guarded write, simple open, and default seek behavior. Two dentries track the enable file and the core-priority file so they can be removed on teardown.

Jailhouse platform initialization overrides pre-vector, timer, MP-table, SMP-config, PCI, CPU and TSC calibration, wallclock, legacy-device, legacy-PIC, and emergency-restart hooks, then locates Jailhouse setup data by walking the boot setup chain, validates header and versioned lengths, imports the payload, and publishes timer port, TSC rate, probe limits, ACPI-disabled state, and serial handling.

Jailhouse detection is based on whether a Jailhouse hypervisor CPUID base is present. Timer initialization derives the local-APIC period from the supplied APIC rate and tick rate. Both CPU and TSC calibration return the precalibrated rate. Wallclock reads return zero time. The x2APIC path forces physical mode when already enabled and triggers selection of the physical driver. SMP parsing registers a fixed local-APIC address and each supplied CPU, then optionally registers a fixed I/O APIC and legacy UART mappings for old setup versions.

Jailhouse PCI setup uses direct access and defaults the last bus to a full scan when no command-line override exists. It registers a memory-mapped configuration window and initializes that mechanism only when a base address is supplied.

Jailhouse UART availability is determined by flag bits in the newer setup payload. The serial fixup enables ports whose bit is set and registers their IRQ, while clearing the base address of disallowed ports. The ISA configurator is installed only for setup versions newer than the first; older builds use an empty workaround.

Saved Jailhouse IRQs use active-high edge-triggered ISA-style entries with identical source and destination numbers. SMP I/O APIC registration uses strict mode with the MP I/O APIC operations. The hypervisor descriptor names Jailhouse, points at detect, platform-init, and x2APIC-availability handlers, and opts out of no-PV handling.
The Jailhouse paravirt predicate, the hypervisor descriptor, and the generic machine-halt wrapper that delegates to the machine operations halt handler are visible to the rest of the kernel.

Jailhouse boot panics when no setup block of its type is found, when the header is shorter than its own header, when the version is zero or has an unexpected compatibility version, or when the payload is shorter than required for its version. Its emergency restart path only logs lack of support and halts.
A jump-label patch value pairs a pointer to replacement bytes with the number of bytes to write. A decoded jump entry is accepted only when its instruction length matches the short or near jump form.

Patch construction generates either a short or near jump encoding toward the entry target and selects the matching no-operation padding. It expects existing memory to contain padding when enabling a jump and jump bytes when disabling one, and treats any other content as fatal corruption.
Jump-label code halts on an unexpected decoded instruction length, on an unhandled patch size, and when the bytes present at the patch address do not match the expected operation before modification.

A jump entry conceptually moves between no-operation and jump encodings. During early boot or explicit init the new bytes are written with the early poke path; otherwise a single SMP text poke is used. Queued updates fall back to the immediate path during boot and otherwise append to a batch that a separate apply operation finishes.
All non-boot jump-label transform, queue, and apply operations hold the text mutex. The inner transform helper assumes the caller already holds that mutex.
The architecture debug directory pointer is globally visible, as are the immediate, queued, and batch-apply jump-label transform operations and the jump-entry size helper.
A setup-data debug node stores a physical address, a type field, and a payload length. Its file table supports read, simple open, and default seek.

Setup-data debug reads reject negative offsets, return end of data at or beyond the payload length, clamp the request to the remaining payload, adjust the physical address for direct payloads while leaving valid indirect payloads unadjusted, map the range as write-back, copy to user space, and distinguish mapping exhaustion from copy faults.
The boot cascade handler is requested on legacy IRQ line two.
Jailhouse registers the local APIC at its conventional fixed physical address and the standard I/O APIC at its conventional fixed physical address.
Jailhouse version-one setup length covers header plus first payload section, and version-two length adds the second payload section.
Only two jump instruction lengths are accepted for patching, corresponding to short and near encodings.
Jailhouse legacy serial handling recognizes four conventional ISA UART base ports in a fixed order.
